title: Broadcom Thor Ultra Ethernet NIC at Hot Chips 2026
gist: Broadcom's Thor Ultra is an 800GbE NIC (5nm, 2.4B transistors, 40-42W) built for AI/HPC scale-up, scale-out, and scale-across Ethernet, offering enhanced RoCE (multipath packet spraying, out-of-order placement, receiver credit-based congestion control) that puts Broadcom in direct 800G competition with Nvidia's ConnectX-8 and AMD's Vulcano, with measured throughput hitting ~97-99% of line rate in early testing.

themes.theme: Competitive positioning in the 800G NIC market

insights.claim: Broadcom's Thor Ultra launch places the company squarely in direct competition with Nvidia's ConnectX-8 and AMD's Vulcano in the emerging 800G AI/HPC NIC market.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Confirms a genuine three-way merchant-silicon race (Broadcom, Nvidia, AMD) for AI NIC market share as hyperscalers scale out GPU/XPU clusters — relevant for assessing Broadcom's networking revenue growth versus Nvidia's networking segment as AI infrastructure spend continues.
insights.quote: This Thor Ultra launch puts Broadcom squarely in the 800G NIC contest alongside NVIDIA's ConnectX-8 and AMD's Vulcano.

insights.claim: Thor Ultra is designed to serve all three layers of AI/HPC Ethernet fabric — scale-up within the rack, scale-out across racks, and scale-across between data centers — with a single shared set of NIC requirements (bandwidth, RDMA, low latency, QoS, virtualization, security, timing, telemetry).
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Broadcom is positioning one NIC architecture to unify all three network scales rather than requiring separate silicon per tier, an efficiency/cost argument aimed at hyperscaler customers evaluating total network buildout cost versus Nvidia's more segmented NVLink/InfiniBand/Ethernet stack.
insights.quote: Ethernet here spans scale-up in the rack, scale-out across racks, and scale-across between data centers, and each layer drives a shared set of NIC requirements.
insights.locator: Broadcom Thor Ultra Ethernet NIC at Hot Chips 2026

insights.claim: The author notes it was 'a little bit awkward' that Broadcom's framing of universal scale-up/out/across Ethernet directly conflicted with Nvidia's own framework (presented later in the same Hot Chips session block) that argues a single general-purpose fabric cannot serve all network scales well.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: A direct architectural disagreement between the two largest AI networking silicon vendors at the same conference is a signal of real strategic tension over whether unified or purpose-built fabrics win — investors should watch which approach hyperscalers actually deploy at scale as the tie-breaker.
insights.quote: It is a little bit awkward given what NVIDIA's framewrok will look like later in this session block.
insights.locator: Broadcom Thor Ultra Ethernet NIC at Hot Chips 2026

themes.theme: Thor Ultra silicon and enhanced RoCE architecture

insights.claim: Thor Ultra is built on 5nm with 2.4 billion transistors in a 27x27mm package at 40-42W max power, pairing a PCIe Gen6 x16 host interface, an 8-port 100G MAC, 256 SR-IOV virtual functions, and 8x 100G SerDes, offloading RoCEv2, stateless packet processing, and inline encryption.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Concrete die specs give a hard baseline for comparing power/transistor efficiency against Nvidia ConnectX-8 and AMD Vulcano NICs in TCO modeling for AI rack deployments.
insights.quote: This is the silicon itself, on 5nm, with a 2.4 billion-transistor count in a 27×27 package, at 40-42W max power.

insights.claim: Thor Ultra's key generational advances over the prior Thor NIC are packet spraying with out-of-order placement, reliability mechanisms beyond simple Go-Back-N, simpler programmable congestion control, and doubled port count with multiplane connectivity.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Multipath packet spraying and multiplane connectivity mirror the same 'multiplane' concept Nvidia champions for Spectrum-X — showing multiplane/multipath fabric design is becoming an industry-standard technique for AI network resilience and load distribution, not a single-vendor differentiator.
insights.quote: What stands out is packet spraying with out-of-order placement, reliability beyond Go-Back-N, simpler, programmable congestion control, and double the ports with multiplane connectivity.

insights.claim: Thor Ultra's enhanced RoCE (eRoCE) supports over 64K queue pairs and sprays packets across up to eight network planes, using selective ACK/NACK-based reliable delivery and per-packet path selection with placement info carried in headers, while the receiver reorders before in-order message delivery.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Fine-grained per-packet multipathing at this queue-pair scale is aimed directly at reducing tail latency/congestion in large AI training/inference clusters — a technical capability investors should treat as table stakes now expected of any competitive 800G AI NIC.
insights.quote: Enhanced RoCE here exceeds 64K queue pairs, with a TruFlow engine and BroadSAFE security.
insights.locator: Ethernet Networking for AI and HPC

insights.claim: Congestion control centers on Receiver Credit-Based Congestion Control, where the receiver hands out credits to active senders (including speculative credits for line-rate startup) while staying aware of ECN, trimming, and CSIG telemetry, all customizable via P4-like match-action engines.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Programmable congestion control via P4-like engines gives hyperscalers the ability to tune network behavior per-workload post-deployment, a flexibility advantage that could matter to cloud providers running heterogeneous AI workloads on shared fabric.
insights.quote: Congestion control centers on Receiver Credit-Based Congestion Control as the eRoCE baseline.

insights.claim: The author repeatedly notes Broadcom describes its packet-processing engines as 'P4-like' rather than standard P4, raising an implicit question about why Broadcom avoided full P4 compatibility.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: A subtle signal that Broadcom's programmability may be more proprietary/limited than a fully open P4 implementation would suggest — worth tracking for whether this creates vendor lock-in or interoperability friction for customers wanting portable network programs across NIC vendors.
insights.quote: I wonder why we have "P4-like" not just P4 engines.

themes.theme: Form factor, GPU integration, and security/manageability

insights.claim: Thor Ultra ships in OCP NIC 3.0 and PCIe form factors with one OSFP112 port (supporting 800G, 2x400G, 4x200G, or 8x100G configurations) or two QSFP112 ports, letting operators reuse a single board across multiple port densities; the board runs 50-55W without optics.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Flexible port configuration on one board lowers hyperscaler inventory/SKU complexity and capex risk when scaling network topologies up or down — a practical deployment advantage in TCO terms.
insights.quote: An OSFP112 port supports 800G, 2x 400G, 4x 200G, or 8x 100G, so operators can reuse a single board across multiple port densities.

insights.claim: For GPU/XPU peer memory transfers, Thor Ultra uses dma-buf for local peer-to-peer DMA and eRoCE for remote transfers, integrating with NCCL, RCCL, and MPI through a verbs provider and xCCL plugins on an upstream dma-buf peer memory model that requires no application modification.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Drop-in compatibility with existing NCCL/RCCL/MPI collective libraries means AI training software written for Nvidia/AMD GPUs can adopt Thor Ultra with minimal integration cost, lowering the switching barrier for hyperscalers evaluating Broadcom versus incumbent NIC vendors.
insights.quote: on an upstream dma-buf peer memory model that leaves applications unmodified.

insights.claim: Security is rooted in silicon with a FUSE-based root of trust, ROM bootstrap loader, authenticated firmware updates, SPDM device attestation, and PSP-based encryption/decryption.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Hardware-rooted security and attestation is increasingly a procurement requirement for hyperscaler and government AI infrastructure deals — a checkbox capability that could gate Broadcom's addressable market for security-sensitive AI customers.
insights.quote: Security starts at the silicon with a FUSE-based root of trust, a ROM bootstrap loader, and authenticated firmware updates.

insights.claim: In initial collective testing across two nodes with 8 Gen5 GPUs each (16 ranks, sixteen 400G links), Thor Ultra achieved all_reduce at 383.93 GB/s and reduce_scatter at 380.23 GB/s against a 400 GB/s ceiling (>96% of line rate), while alltoall was a clear outlier at only 84.62 GB/s.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Near-line-rate all_reduce/reduce_scatter performance is a strong early proof point for Thor Ultra's viability in real GPU training clusters, though the alltoall shortfall flags a potential weak spot for MoE-style expert-routing workloads that rely heavily on alltoall communication.
insights.quote: the chart puts all_reduce at 383.93 GB/s and reduce_scatter at 380.23 GB/s against a 400 GB/s ceiling, while alltoall is the clear outlier at 84.62 GB/s.
insights.locator: Collective Performance – Initial Data on a Gen5 GPU Platform

insights.claim: On TCP, Thor Ultra reached 791 Gbps unidirectional (98.9% of the 800G link) with 16 parallel iperf3 flows, and about 1.51 Tbps aggregate bidirectional throughput, saturating near-linearly up to eight flows.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Near-saturation TCP throughput at 800G validates the core NIC data path performance independent of RDMA-specific optimizations, supporting Broadcom's line-rate claims under real test conditions.
insights.quote: iperf3 on a Gen6 CPU with 512 GB DDR5-8000 hits 791 Gbps unidirectional at 16 parallel flows, about 98.9% of the 800G link.

insights.claim: For RDMA writes, Thor Ultra saturates at 781 Gbps unidirectional and 1558 Gbps bidirectional (97.6% of the 1.6Tb/s aggregate), reaching about 88% of line rate by 32KB messages and within 3% of peak by 128KB messages.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Message-size-dependent throughput ramp is directly relevant to AI training efficiency, since gradient/activation message sizes vary — near-peak performance by 128KB suggests good efficiency for typical large-tensor AI communication patterns.
insights.quote: the bidirectional path reaches 1558 Gbps, about 97.6% of the 1.6 Tb/s aggregate and roughly double the unidirectional rate.
insights.locator: Thor Ultra Throughput for RDMA Writes
